module

public import Mathlib.Combinatorics.SimpleGraph.Maps
public import Mathlib.Data.Set.Card

@[expose] public section

namespace SimpleGraph

variable {V : Type*}

/-- `G` is a **unique subgraph** of `H` if there is exactly one subgraph of `H` isomorphic to
`G`. Subgraphs of `H` are taken in the spanning sense: elements `G' ≤ H` of the lattice
`SimpleGraph V`, i.e. subsets of the edges of `H` (not necessarily induced). -/
def IsUniqueSubgraph (G H : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∃! G' : SimpleGraph V, G' ≤ H ∧ Nonempty (G.Iso G')

/-- The number of distinct unique subgraphs of `H`: the number of isomorphism classes of graphs
that occur exactly once as a subgraph of `H`. Each such class contains exactly one subgraph
`G ≤ H` (uniqueness forbids a second isomorphic copy), so counting those representatives counts
the classes. -/
noncomputable def uniqueSubgraphCount (H : SimpleGraph V) : ℕ :=
  {G : SimpleGraph V | G ≤ H ∧ IsUniqueSubgraph G H}.ncard

end SimpleGraph

findings.description: The definition accepts arbitrary vertex types but uses `Set.ncard`, so it can return 0 when there are infinitely many distinct unique spanning subgraphs. This contradicts its unqualified description as their number. For a concrete allowed input, take H to be the disjoint union of one cycle Cₖ for each k ≥ 3. Let Gₖ retain only the edges of Cₖ, leaving every other vertex isolated. Any spanning subgraph of H isomorphic to Gₖ must use the unique cycle component of length k, hence must equal Gₖ. Thus all Gₖ satisfy the counted predicate, the counted set is infinite, and `uniqueSubgraphCount H = 0`. This does not affect the current problem-426 use on `Fin n`.
findings.source_evidence: The definition's docstring, SubgraphIsomorphism.lean:33–36, promises the number of unique-subgraph isomorphism classes without a finiteness qualification. Mathlib/Data/Set/Card.lean explicitly documents `Set.ncard` as having the junk value 0 on infinite sets and proves `Set.Infinite.ncard`. The neighbouring `SimpleGraph.copyCount` in Mathlib/Combinatorics/SimpleGraph/Copy.lean assumes a finite host. Bradač–Christoph, arXiv:2410.16233, §1, likewise introduces the counting function for an n-vertex host.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `[Finite V]` to `uniqueSubgraphCount`, which preserves all current uses and guarantees that the counted set is finite. If infinite hosts are intended, use `Set.encard` with codomain `ℕ∞` instead.

reformulations.difference: For finite graphs on the same vertex type, the definition uses the lattice of spanning graphs `G' ≤ H`, rather than quantifying over Mathlib's vertex-and-edge subgraphs `S : H.Subgraph`.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: An isomorphism from G on finite V to S.coe induces an injection V → V whose image is S.verts. Finiteness makes it surjective, so S spans H. The conversions between spanning subgraphs and graphs below H preserve isomorphism and uniqueness. Both this equivalence and `IsUniqueSubgraph G H ↔ H.copyCount G = 1` were proved in the scratch file. The infinite-graph spanning convention is explicitly documented and was not treated as ordinary unrestricted subgraph uniqueness.

reformulations.difference: On finite hosts, it counts actual spanning representatives below H rather than forming an explicit quotient by graph isomorphism.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Each isomorphism class occurring uniquely has exactly one representative below H, and that representative itself satisfies IsUniqueSubgraph. Conversely, two counted representatives that are isomorphic must be equal. Consequently the representative count equals the count of unique spanning isomorphism classes. The injectivity claim was proved in Lean; the complete quotient-count equality was not.

reformulations.difference: The theorem negates a positive lower bound occurring at arbitrarily large n for the spanning count. The source's resolution states that the maximum count of unique subgraphs of all orders is little-o of A(n) = 2^(n choose 2)/n!.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For an n-vertex host, let S(H) be the spanning count and U(H) the all-orders count. Then 0 ≤ U(H) − S(H) ≤ Σ_{k<n} a(k), where a(k) counts unlabelled k-vertex graphs. Bradač–Christoph explicitly show in §2.1 that this sum is o(A(n)). Thus the normalized maxima of S and U tend to zero simultaneously. Since A(n)>0 and the counts are nonnegative, convergence to zero is equivalent to the negation of a fixed positive lower bound holding frequently. The general frequent/limit equivalence was proved in Lean, but the full asymptotic enumeration reduction was not.
